clinical_knowledge.topic: Anterior Mediastinal Thymoma with Myasthenia Gravis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Anterior Mediastinal Thymoma with Myasthenia Gravis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes preoperative optimization of myasthenia gravis (pyridostigmine, and IVIG/plasmapheresis or corticosteroids when indicated) to reduce the risk of postoperative myasthenic crisis, followed by median sternotomy thymectomy with en bloc resection of the encapsulated thymoma, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty chewing, and anterior mediastinal mass on CT

Key HPI features: 44F with Myasthenia Gravis presenting with ptosis and diplopia with chest CT demonstrating a 5 cm well-encapsulated anterior mediastinal thymoma undergoing median sternotomy resection.

Objective/Exam findings: Ptosis worsens with sustained upward gaze (fatigability); positive ice-pack test. Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies positive. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response. Chest CT confirms a 5 cm well-encapsulated anterior mediastinal mass consistent with thymoma, without local invasion. Pulmonary function tests show normal forced vital capacity with no evidence of respiratory muscle weakness at rest.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Anterior Mediastinal Thymoma with Myasthenia Gravis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Isolated ocular myasthenia (without thymoma) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Difficulty swallowing or breathing — myasthenic crisis, a neuromuscular emergency.
management_principles: Optimize myasthenia gravis medically (pyridostigmine; consider IVIG/plasmapheresis or corticosteroids preoperatively if indicated) to reduce risk of postoperative myasthenic crisis
Proceed with median sternotomy thymectomy for en bloc resection of the encapsulated thymoma, with anesthetic avoidance of neuromuscular blocking agents where possible
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 44F with myasthenia gravis presenting with progressive fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty chewing, found to have a 5 cm well-encapsulated anterior mediastinal thymoma on chest CT.
reference_soap.objective: Ptosis worsens with sustained upward gaze (fatigability); positive ice-pack test. Anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies positive. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows a decremental response. Chest CT confirms a 5 cm well-encapsulated anterior mediastinal mass consistent with thymoma, without local invasion. Pulmonary function tests show normal forced vital capacity with no evidence of respiratory muscle weakness at rest.
reference_soap.assessment: Anterior mediastinal thymoma (5 cm, well-encapsulated, likely Masaoka-Koga stage I) associated with generalized myasthenia gravis.
reference_soap.plan: Optimize myasthenia gravis medically (pyridostigmine; consider IVIG/plasmapheresis or corticosteroids preoperatively if indicated) to reduce risk of postoperative myasthenic crisis. Proceed with median sternotomy thymectomy for en bloc resection of the encapsulated thymoma, with anesthetic avoidance of neuromuscular blocking agents where possible.

learning_objectives: Recognize the fatigable pattern of ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar weakness characteristic of myasthenia gravis and its association with thymoma
Formulate a prioritized differential diagnosis for an anterior mediastinal mass, including thymoma, lymphoma, and germ cell tumor
Select appropriate diagnostic studies (AChR antibody testing, repetitive nerve stimulation, chest CT, pulmonary function tests) before thymectomy
Explain the rationale for preoperative myasthenia optimization and anesthetic precautions to reduce the risk of postoperative myasthenic crisis

teaching.diagnosis: Anterior Mediastinal Thymoma with Myasthenia Gravis
teaching.one_liner: A thymus gland tumor, strongly associated with myasthenia gravis, causing ptosis and double vision from autoimmune neuromuscular junction dysfunction — treated with surgical resection via median sternotomy.
red_flags: Difficulty swallowing or breathing — myasthenic crisis, a neuromuscular emergency

must_ask.say: Does the eyelid drooping or double vision get worse as the day goes on?
Do you have trouble chewing or swallowing, especially later in a meal?
Does your weakness improve after resting?
How long have you had these symptoms?

history.answer: My eyelids have been drooping more and more, and I keep seeing double, especially later in the day.
It started gradually about two months ago, and the drooping and double vision have slowly gotten worse.
Both of my eyelids droop, though the left eye is often a bit worse than the right.
The double vision comes and goes throughout the day, but it has been happening every single day for the past several weeks.
My vision itself isn't blurry or dark; things just split into two clear side-by-side images.
Both close-up reading and distant objects become double when my eyes get tired, and new glasses didn't help at all.
I haven't had issues with glare or halos around streetlights, but driving at night is tough because of the double images.
No, I have never seen any spots, flashing lights, or dark curtains over my eyes.
Yes, I see two distinct images side by side, and the moment I cover either eye, the second image goes away.
My eyelids are barely droopy when I wake up, but by late afternoon and evening they feel very heavy and hard to keep open.
My jaw muscles get very tired and weak whenever I chew tough foods like steak, but I can swallow liquids and food without choking.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath, chest tightness, or trouble breathing at all.
No, my eyes don't hurt, there is no pain when looking around, and they aren't red.
I haven't had any new headaches, tenderness over my temples, jaw stiffness, or shoulder pain.
My arms and legs feel fine without any numbness or tingling, though my voice can sound a bit weak after talking for a long time.
No, I have never had any injury or hit to my eyes or head.
No, I have never had high blood pressure or diabetes, and my last routine eye checkup was completely normal.
No, I don't have any heart rhythm problems, carotid artery disease, or other vascular issues.
I wear mild glasses for nearsightedness, but I have never had glaucoma, cataracts, or any eye surgery.
I have never taken steroids, hydroxychloroquine, or any other medications known to affect vision.
No one in my family has had glaucoma, macular degeneration, or any eye or muscle disorders.
It makes reading and evening driving very frustrating, and I have to rest my eyes frequently, but I haven't had any falls.
A recent chest CT scan showed a 5-centimeter mass in the front of my chest, which the doctor said is a tumor in my thymus gland.
I think this tumor in my chest is what's causing my droopy eyelids and double vision, and I'm hoping having it removed will cure everything.
I'm really terrified about having my breastbone split open and being in horrible pain for weeks afterward.
I was recently diagnosed with myasthenia gravis, but I have no other chronic medical problems.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital before.
I take pyridostigmine prescribed by my neurologist, and I don't take any other medications, over-the-counter pills, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink a glass of wine on rare social occasions, maybe once a month.
I work as an office administrator, stay physically active, and live with my husband.
My menstrual periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my last period started two weeks ago, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert and comfortable at rest with mild bilateral eyelid drooping, in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, body temperature 36.7°C.

Visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally; pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light without relative afferent pupillary defect; visual fields are full to confrontation; bilateral ptosis worsens on sustained upward gaze; binocular diplopia occurs on lateral and upward gaze; ice-pack test is positive; funduscopy reveals clear media, sharp optic disc margins, and normal retina.
Temporal arteries are non-tender and pulsatile bilaterally without thickening or nodularity.
Facial sensation is intact, facial expression is symmetric, palate elevates symmetrically with normal gag reflex, and tongue protrudes midline without dysarthria.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout both upper and lower extremities at rest.
Biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ bilaterally, and plantar responses are flexor.
Clear vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with good air entry and no wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Regular heart rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops appreciated.
